title: Children in flood-hit Nepal grapple with loss, cling to hope - The Korea Herald
description: Children in flood-hit Nepal grapple with loss, cling to hope  The Korea Herald
publisher.title: The Korea Herald
full_article:
Children, separated from their parents from the flash floods, study at a temporary learning center run by Save the Children charity in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Friday. (AFP-Yonhap)

NUWAKOT, Nepal (AFP) -- At 12, Nepali schoolgirl Ritu Maya Tamang has already learned how a close-knit family can be torn apart in a matter of minutes.

Tamang is among more than 500 children separated from their parents by the catastrophic August 26 flooding that hit the China-Nepal border, sweeping away homes, bridges and houses.

Nepal's disaster agency said Friday that 1,385 bodies had been retrieved, while 5,130 people remained missing. In China, state media says 43 people are dead and 519 missing.

The flood that first hit Nepal's high-altitude Rasuwa district claimed the life of Tamang's mother, but her body is yet to be found.

Tamang's younger sister is now battling pneumonia in hospital, and her father stays by her bedside.

While her life has been upended by the country's worst-ever flood disaster, one thing remains unchanged -- Tamang still wants to become a doctor.

"I get nightmares about the flood," the shy seventh grader said as she finished an essay in her neat handwriting at a temporary learning centre run by Save the Children charity in Nuwakot district. "But I have dreams." Nearby, children -- some of them younger than five -- put finishing touches to colourful crayon drawings.

The memory of the day the floods struck is fresh in Tamang's mind.

Her mother, a housekeeper, was at work at a hydropower project office next to the Trishuli River.

"When the water came gushing, my mother could not escape it. I survived because I was at school," said Tamang, her eyes glistening with tears.

The only keepsake that Tamang has of her mother is a black face mask that she had tucked in her bag.

Save the Children says at least 540 children have been separated from their parents, and are living along with thousands others in relief camps in flood-affected areas, according to a preliminary assessment.

In one of the tented learning centres, teacher Shanti Sapkota said when the children first arrived, many were in a state of shock and panic.

"They would say that 'my house has been taken away,' 'my father has been swept away' or 'my mother has been swept away,'" Sapkota told Agence France-Presse.

"But they are slowly moving on from that state of mind." Nepal's government has said it will guarantee education through high school for affected children, with support ranging from residential care to full scholarships.

Along with its stakeholders, the government has committed to establishing a $6.5-million scholarship fund for some 1,000 students affected by the floods.

"We are giving priority to children who have lost their guardians," said education minister Sasmit Pokharel.

"We will identify what kind of support each child needs. ... We will stand by them," he said on Monday.

At the Nuwakot learning center, psychologist Ekta Shreshtha said the children were easily triggered by any strange person or noise.

"It is still early days but from my observation, many of them are having trouble sleeping and have retreated into a shell," she told AFP.

"We try to keep them distracted with toys and other fun activities that help them forget their trauma for some time," she said.

"But their whole life is ahead of them. The pain is going to come back again."

Temporary centers for children

title: Nepal takes its floods to the U.N. — and asks who will pay - The Japan Times
description: Nepal takes its floods to the U.N. — and asks who will pay  The Japan Times
publisher.title: The Japan Times
full_article:
Nepal’s recent catastrophic floods, which have killed more than 1,340 people and left nearly 5,000 missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency, could change the way the world confronts the mounting climate-driven losses of developing nations.

Later this month, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah will make his first foreign trip six months after taking office, traveling to New York to lead a small delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. He will seek climate justice for Nepal and international support following the disaster along the Nepal-China border. Shah is scheduled to speak during the U.N. General Assembly’s general debate on Sept. 24.

The floods struck Aug. 26, when a mass of water, mud and ice broke loose near the Nepal‑China border and swept through villages, devastating homes, infrastructure and the people who lived and were visiting there. Nepal observed a national day of mourning 13 days after the disaster.

On the Chinese side, authorities there reported 43 dead and 519 missing at the time of this writing. Rescue teams have continued pulling survivors from the wreckage in recent days, including a Chinese man freed from a tunnel at a hydropower plant and a 64-year-old Nepali woman recovered from the top floor of a mud-buried building.

Japan has its own stake in the recovery effort. Five Japanese nationals remain unaccounted for and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi pressed Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, in a phone call to intensify the search for them. Tokyo has since sent blankets, tents and other relief supplies through the Japanese Embassy in Kathmandu, and Japanese forensic specialists are working alongside teams from India, China, Singapore and South Korea to identify recovered remains.

Khanal had originally been expected to lead Nepal’s delegation to the U.N. General Assembly, but in the wake of one of the deadliest disasters in the country’s recent history, the government reconsidered and Shah opted to lead it himself. The Prime Minister’s Office has instructed the Foreign Ministry to keep the delegation small.

Nepal’s Finance Ministry has already written to the U.N.’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, requesting emergency financial assistance. The ministry is framing it as a special request because the fund’s board does not ordinarily consider losses of this scale on its December agenda. The ministry has also argued that Nepal is absorbing outsized damage despite contributing very little to global carbon emissions.

Experts have attributed the flooding to a massive rockslide in the Himalayas, a hazard that climate change is making more frequent as the region warms. Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, 21 of which have been flagged as potentially dangerous given their physical characteristics and the populations living downstream.

Nepal accounts for roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The question its delegation intends to put to the General Assembly is whether the nations responsible for the bulk of that pollution owe anything to communities now absorbing its consequences.

The Loss and Damage Fund was created to help developing nations cope with climate-driven losses, but it remains underfunded, in large part because the United States and other wealthy donors have been reluctant to contribute. Pledges to the fund have totaled roughly $768 million since its creation, and the board has approved only a $250 million pilot package to cover claims through 2026, with individual grants capped at $20 million.

Independent estimates put the annual cost of loss and damage in developing countries at $400 billion to $580 billion by the end of the decade, rising toward $1 trillion once noneconomic losses are factored in. The fund holds well under one-tenth of 1% of what is actually needed in a given year. Washington’s withdrawal of its own $17.5 million pledge earlier this year has not helped and other wealthy donors are said to be watching that retreat closely.

Nepal’s own government bears some responsibility as well. Hydropower plants were built directly in the path of volatile glacial rivers without adequate early-warning systems, and questions are already surfacing in Kathmandu over whether disaster preparedness kept pace with the country’s infrastructure ambitions.

Critics will say Nepal is asking foreign capitals to underwrite its own planning failures. But domestic mismanagement does not settle the separate question of whether nations responsible for the overwhelming share of global emissions owe something to communities now living with the physical loss.

None of this guarantees Nepal will secure the funding it is seeking. Loss-and-damage finance remains chronically thin, and the wealthy nations Shah will address in New York have spent three decades treating climate compensation as a line item to be minimized rather than an obligation to be met. His appearance at the General Assembly will test whether a framework built after Pakistan’s 2022 floods and Nepal’s own 2024 glacial lake outbursts can hold up under a live crisis of this scale.

The fund itself is barely three years old. Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022, after floods submerged nearly a third of Pakistan and killed more than 1,700 people. It did not become operational until COP29 in Baku two years later, and its first call for disbursements opened only in December 2025, built around grants for discrete pilot projects rather than a single disaster with a death toll in the thousands.

Whether Nepal’s request forces the fund to stretch beyond that design, or simply exposes how far short it still falls, is the question New York will have to answer.

Brabim Karki is an author and businessman based in Nepal. He is the owner of Mero Tribune media.

title: Hydropower Worker Survives 10 Days in Flooded Tunnel in Nepal - UA.NEWS
description: Hydropower Worker Survives 10 Days in Flooded Tunnel in Nepal  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, Sanjay Saha, a worker on a hydropower project, was rescued from a flooded tunnel after 10 days in darkness. He became trapped during the catastrophic flood on August 26, caused by the collapse of a glacial mountain on the border between China and Nepal.

As Channel NewsAsia reports, citing AFP, the 30-year-old Saha was pulled from the tunnel on September 4. After being rescued, he first asked rescuers how much time had passed. According to him, he believed he had been trapped for only several days.

Flooding at hydropower facilities

Saha was among hundreds of workers at several hydropower projects affected by the flood. He said that workers received a warning about the approaching water and tried to evacuate their colleagues, but there was not enough time. According to him, within minutes the tunnel was engulfed by raging water with waves several meters high.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The Nepalese government linked the scale of the disaster to the consequences of rising global temperatures for the Himalayas. According to the data cited in the report, the disaster claimed at least 1,429 lives, while more than 5,640 people were considered missing; most of them were in Nepal.

Muddy water and contact with a colleague

Saha said he had no clean water and drank muddy water. In the darkness, he prayed and recited Hindu mantras, which, he said, helped him not lose hope. Nearby, 45-year-old worker Kabir Maharjan also survived. The men were separated but were able to speak to each other.

After several days in a Kathmandu hospital, Saha was returning to his home district of Saptari. He urged that search and rescue operations in the tunnels not be stopped. According to the outlet, rescuers saved another worker from China on September 5, but since then they have recorded no signs of life from other people.

title: The search dog helping find bodies buried by Nepal’s floods - The Kathmandu Post
description: The search dog helping find bodies buried by Nepal’s floods  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The search for people still missing after the Rasuwa floods is continuing, with rescuers from the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police combing through mud, collapsed buildings, debris-strewn riverbanks and tunnels.

But they are not relying on human eyes alone.

Trained search dogs are also being used to scour the disaster zone. One of them, Samba, a Labrador brought to Nepal from India and trained to detect the scent of human remains, has helped rescuers locate around 20 bodies.

Samba is part of the Armed Police Force’s K-9 unit, whose trained dogs have been working in the flood-hit areas since August 26. Their job is to identify places where people may be buried beneath soil or rubble and alert the teams carrying out the searches.

When Samba picks up the scent of a person beneath the ground, he barks to signal his handlers. The rescuers then begin digging at the spot.

The dog works with a primary handler and an assistant, both members of the security forces trained to read his behaviour. Samba may slow down, focus intently on a particular area, sit down or scratch at the ground with his paws.

Those movements can help the handlers determine where rescuers should dig.

Samba has so far helped locate around 20 bodies in the Trishuli area and at Timure in Rasuwa. After days of searching through the wreckage, his work has given rescue teams another way to find people buried beneath the debris.

The Armed Police Force has deployed five trained dogs, including Samba, in the flood-hit areas. Nepal Police has deployed six more, while the Nepali Army also has trained dogs used for various search and rescue operations.

title: Nepal disaster highlights need for multi-hazard assessment of Himalayas: Senior Geologist - BusinessLine
description: Nepal disaster highlights need for multi-hazard assessment of Himalayas: Senior Geologist  BusinessLine
publisher.title: BusinessLine
full_article:
The Himalayas face the threat of a cascading disaster, where a single high-altitude calamity can trigger avalanches, block rivers and unleash flash floods, rapidly magnifying destruction downstream -- a danger laid bare by Nepal's recent catastrophe, said a senior Geological Survey of India official.

Therefore, Himalayan hazards cannot be assessed in isolation, he pointed out and stressed the need for combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

A case in point is the Nepal disaster that appears to have involved cascading processes.

Satellite analysis identified an impoundment near the Langtang Lirung ice-rock avalanche site, with imagery of August 28 showing an approximately 11-hectare water impounded area.

This provides evidence that the initial ice-rock failure was associated with temporary obstruction and water accumulation in the river system, said Pradeep Singh, the ADG of Policy Support System at the Geological Survey of India.

The flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal. The Bhotekoshi river carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, roads and bridges and killing more than 1,300 people.

Singh stressed the need to identify unstable mountain systems before they turn into catastrophic events.

"A single instability at high elevation can initiate a sequence involving an avalanche, landslide or glacier failure, river blockage, dam-break type release, debris flow and downstream flooding. Such processes can interact and amplify one another," he told PTI here.

The geologist said the priority should be systematic scientific screening of potentially high-risk areas, particularly locations where a high-altitude failure could rapidly enter a river and affect populations and infrastructure downstream.

"The immediate priority should be a systematic, science-based screening of potentially high-risk source areas, rather than assuming that a similar catastrophic event will occur everywhere." He pointed out that such screening should prioritise rapidly deforming glacier margins and glacier-rock systems, unstable and moraine-dammed glacial lakes, steep and fractured rock slopes, locations showing persistent or accelerating deformation in satellite observations, and valleys where a high-altitude failure could rapidly propagate downstream.

Glacial lakes are formed by melting glaciers accumulating in depressions on or near the glacier’s surface. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods occur when these lakes suddenly burst open due to factors such as excessive water accumulation or earthquakes. One such outburst in Sikkim in October 2023 resulted in at least 60 fatalities and extensive damage in four districts.

Singh said, "Satellite observations can potentially provide valuable precursor information, particularly where progressive deformation or acceleration occurs before failure. However, a detected increase in movement indicates that the particular slope is in distress; however, the failure will occur on reaching the limit equilibrium condition, which may be difficult to predict." The answer lies in combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

Singh asserted that the most effective approach was not to rely on a single satellite indicator, but to integrate multi-temporal InSAR, optical feature tracking, DEM differencing, field instrumentation and ground observations.

This would allow authorities to build a regional inventory of anomalous or rapidly deforming glacier-rock, moraine and slope systems and focus detailed investigations and monitoring on locations with potentially serious downstream consequences.

"The objective should be to identify potentially unstable systems early, understand how they may fail, estimate their possible downstream effects and establish an appropriate level of monitoring and preparedness." Singh said the concern was particularly relevant for the Indian segment of the Himalayas because the region combines glaciers, steep and fractured rock slopes, permafrost-affected terrain, glacial lakes, unstable moraines and rapidly flowing rivers, while settlements and critical infrastructure are often concentrated downstream.

"The key shift required is from hazard-by-hazard assessment to source-to-impact multi-hazard assessment. It allows authorities to understand not only where instability may occur, but also what could happen next and who or what may be exposed downstream,” he said.

He, however, cautioned against interpreting the Nepal disaster as proof that every Himalayan town in India faces an imminent glacier-related catastrophe. "Risk in India is highly site-specific and depends on local geology, slope stability, glacier and glacial-lake conditions, hydrology, climate, terrain and patterns of human development." He said there were nevertheless reasons for vigilance on changing glacier conditions, expanding or unstable glacial lakes and moraines, possible permafrost degradation at high elevations, steep and fractured slopes, intense rainfall, landslides and debris flows, as well as increasing infrastructure, settlement and tourism in valleys.

GSI is undertaking landslide susceptibility assessments and glaciological studies in the Himalayas, Singh said, adding that these data should be integrated with satellite deformation monitoring, glacial-lake inventories, geophysical studies and flood and debris-flow modelling.

GSI studies of nine Himalayan glaciers have recorded overall negative average annual specific mass balance, indicative of substantial glacier mass wastage under changing climatic conditions.

"For India, the appropriate response is not alarm, but science-based preparedness. The objective is not to eliminate the mountains' natural processes, but to understand them better, identify highly vulnerable areas, reduce exposure and improve available response time.

"With sustained scientific monitoring, improved data sharing, appropriate land-use planning, robust infrastructure and community preparedness, risks can be better managed," Singh added.

title: Nepal Army chief heads to Beijing for Xiangshan Forum and China talks - India Today
description: Nepal Army chief heads to Beijing for Xiangshan Forum and China talks  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Nepal Army chief Ashok Raj Sigdel left for Beijing on Sunday on a week-long official visit to China at the invitation of the Chinese government, according to an official statement. During the September 13-19 visit, he will attend the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum, a key platform for international security and defence dialogue.

The Nepal Army said the visit is expected to strengthen military ties between Nepal and China and support Nepal's foreign policy through military diplomacy. During Sigdel's absence, Nepal Army Chief of Staff Pradeep Jung KC will serve as acting chief of the Nepal Army.

The 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum will be held from September 15 to 17 at the Beijing International Convention Centre. Its theme this year is "Build Consensus on Stability, Advance Security Governance Together". The forum will bring together senior defence officials, military leaders, heads of international and regional organisations, and experts and scholars.

Sigdel is also expected to address the forum, The Kathmandu Post reported. During his visit, he is expected to meet senior Chinese military officials and discuss future military cooperation, including preparations for the next edition of the joint Nepal-China military exercise, Sagarmatha Friendship, the report said.

title: Families await news of 55 Malaysians missing after Nepal floods - mediaselangor.com
description: Families await news of 55 Malaysians missing after Nepal floods  mediaselangor.com
publisher.title: mediaselangor.com
full_article:
SHAH ALAM, Sept 13 – The families and next-of-kin of 55 Malaysians who remain missing following the massive floods in Nepal continue to await the latest updates from the authorities, 19 days after the incident occurred.

The wife of Senior Fire Officer II Mohd Fakhrul Munir Mohd Isa, Hani Othman, said the families have yet to receive results regarding the DNA matching between relatives in Malaysia and the remains of victims in Nepal, *Berita Harian* reported.

However, Hani understood that the process is still ongoing.

"There are no updates yet on the DNA matching test. But I am told it is still in progress.

“I am still hoping for a miracle, yet I remain resigned to whatever outcome may come," she said when contacted.

On August 28, Hani reportedly flew to Kathmandu on her own to obtain direct updates on the search operations for her husband and other victims who remained out of contact.

She said she wanted to be closer to the search operations rather than simply waiting for updates from Malaysia.

When asked about the conclusion of the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (SMART) MAS-01 mission in Nepal, Hani declined to comment further.

"I don't know how to comment. I have to be mindful of various parties; this issue is very sensitive," she said.

P. Sivan, 72, the father of Rajita Sivan said that DNA samples from the next-of-kin have already been collected, and the family is now awaiting further updates from Wisma Putra.

"The DNA has been collected. We are waiting for news from Wisma Putra. I hope (the victims) are found so that the DNA matching can be carried out.

"If they are found alive, it would be a miracle," he said.

A total of 55 Malaysians were reported to be out of contact following the disaster.

title: 'Nepal's mountains are not closed,' says new NTB board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu - The Tourism Times
description: 'Nepal's mountains are not closed,' says new NTB board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal’s mountains remain open to climbers and trekkers despite the recent devastation in Rasuwa and along the Bhotekoshi corridor, said newly appointed Nepal Tourism Board member Pemba Sherpa from Manaslu Base Camp.

Sherpa, who is in the base camp on behalf of the NTB to monitor mountaineering activity, said more than 400 climbers were currently there as the autumn climbing season got underway.

“Our mountains are not closed. We are open,” Sherpa said in a message from the base camp, urging international visitors not to stop travelling to Nepal following the recent floods.

According to the Department of Tourism, 451 climbers have received permits to climb Manaslu this autumn, making it by far the busiest mountain in Nepal’s current climbing season. Sherpa said the number of climbers and mountain guides involved in the season would exceed 1,000.

His remarks come weeks after devastating floods in Rasuwa and along the Bhotekoshi River disrupted communities and raised concerns about the impact on Nepal’s tourism industry.

“Please do visit our country, love our country, continue your climbing, continue your trekking, continue your journey,” Sherpa said. “We will support you.”

He said continued travel to Nepal would benefit the country while also supporting guides and other tourism workers whose livelihoods depend on trekking and mountaineering.

“This will be beneficial for the country, beneficial for the cause of flood relief and beneficial for our guides and their livelihood,” he said.

Sherpa is one of five private-sector members recently appointed to the NTB board. A director at 8K Expeditions, he has nearly 15 years of experience in Nepal’s tourism industry, including managing trekking and mountaineering expeditions and working as a general manager at a trekking agency.

Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain at 8,163 metres, has emerged as the main focus of Nepal’s autumn climbing season. The September 11 royalty report shows 451 climbers have been authorised to climb the mountain, generating $1.353 million in royalties.

title: Nepal Floods: 'Himalayas At Risk Of Cascading Disasters' - Rediff
description: Nepal Floods: 'Himalayas At Risk Of Cascading Disasters'  Rediff
publisher.title: Rediff
full_article:
Following Nepal's devastating floods, a senior Geological Survey of India official warns that the Himalayas are highly susceptible to cascading disasters, urging integrated scientific monitoring and preparedness to mitigate widespread destruction.

IMAGE: Members of the Nepal's Armed Police Force cross the Trishuli River via a temporary ropeway, in the aftermath of deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Devighat, Bagmati Province, Nepal. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

Key Points The Himalayas face a significant threat from cascading disasters, where a single high-altitude event can trigger a series of destructive phenomena like avalanches, river blockages, and flash floods, as seen in Nepal.

Assessing Himalayan hazards requires an integrated approach, combining satellite observations with on-ground field investigations and instrumentation to identify unstable mountain systems early.

Systematic scientific screening of high-risk areas, including deforming glaciers, unstable glacial lakes, and fractured rock slopes, is crucial for proactive disaster management.

The Indian Himalayas are particularly vulnerable due to their complex geology, rapidly flowing rivers, and concentrated settlements downstream, necessitating a shift to source-to-impact multi-hazard assessments.

Science-based preparedness, including sustained monitoring, data sharing, land-use planning, and community readiness, is essential to manage risks effectively rather than succumbing to alarm.

The Himalayas face the threat of a cascading disaster, where a single high-altitude calamity can trigger avalanches, block rivers and unleash flash floods, rapidly magnifying destruction downstream -- a danger laid bare by Nepal's recent catastrophe, said a senior Geological Survey of India official.

Therefore, Himalayan hazards cannot be assessed in isolation, he pointed out and stressed the need for combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

A case in point is the Nepal disaster that appears to have involved cascading processes.

Satellite analysis identified an impoundment near the Langtang Lirung ice-rock avalanche site, with imagery of August 28 showing an approximately 11-hectare water impounded area. This provides evidence that the initial ice-rock failure was associated with temporary obstruction and water accumulation in the river system, said Pradeep Singh, the ADG of Policy Support System at the Geological Survey of India.

The flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

The Bhotekoshi river carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, roads and bridges and killing more than 1,300 people.

Understanding Cascading Disasters in the Himalayas

Singh stressed the need to identify unstable mountain systems before they turn into catastrophic events.

"A single instability at high elevation can initiate a sequence involving an avalanche, landslide or glacier failure, river blockage, dam-break type release, debris flow and downstream flooding. Such processes can interact and amplify one another," he told PTI.

The geologist said the priority should be systematic scientific screening of potentially high-risk areas, particularly locations where a high-altitude failure could rapidly enter a river and affect populations and infrastructure downstream.

"The immediate priority should be a systematic, science-based screening of potentially high-risk source areas, rather than assuming that a similar catastrophic event will occur everywhere."

He pointed out that such screening should prioritise rapidly deforming glacier margins and glacier-rock systems, unstable and moraine-dammed glacial lakes, steep and fractured rock slopes, locations showing persistent or accelerating deformation in satellite observations, and valleys where a high-altitude failure could rapidly propagate downstream.

Glacial lakes are formed by melting glaciers accumulating in depressions on or near the glacier's surface. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods occur when these lakes suddenly burst open due to factors such as excessive water accumulation or earthquakes.

One such outburst in Sikkim in October 2023 resulted in at least 60 fatalities and extensive damage in four districts.

Integrating Satellite Data and Ground Investigations

Singh said, "Satellite observations can potentially provide valuable precursor information, particularly where progressive deformation or acceleration occurs before failure. However, a detected increase in movement indicates that the particular slope is in distress; however, the failure will occur on reaching the limit equilibrium condition, which may be difficult to predict."

The answer lies in combining satellite-based observations with field investigations and ground instrumentation.

Singh asserted that the most effective approach was not to rely on a single satellite indicator, but to integrate multi-temporal InSAR, optical feature tracking, DEM differencing, field instrumentation and ground observations.

This would allow authorities to build a regional inventory of anomalous or rapidly deforming glacier-rock, moraine and slope systems and focus detailed investigations and monitoring on locations with potentially serious downstream consequences.

"The objective should be to identify potentially unstable systems early, understand how they may fail, estimate their possible downstream effects and establish an appropriate level of monitoring and preparedness."

Himalayan Vulnerabilities and Preparedness in India

Singh said the concern was particularly relevant for the Indian segment of the Himalayas because the region combines glaciers, steep and fractured rock slopes, permafrost-affected terrain, glacial lakes, unstable moraines and rapidly flowing rivers, while settlements and critical infrastructure are often concentrated downstream.

"The key shift required is from hazard-by-hazard assessment to source-to-impact multi-hazard assessment. It allows authorities to understand not only where instability may occur, but also what could happen next and who or what may be exposed downstream," he said.

He, however, cautioned against interpreting the Nepal disaster as proof that every Himalayan town in India faces an imminent glacier-related catastrophe.

"Risk in India is highly site-specific and depends on local geology, slope stability, glacier and glacial-lake conditions, hydrology, climate, terrain and patterns of human development."

He said there were nevertheless reasons for vigilance on changing glacier conditions, expanding or unstable glacial lakes and moraines, possible permafrost degradation at high elevations, steep and fractured slopes, intense rainfall, landslides and debris flows, as well as increasing infrastructure, settlement and tourism in valleys.

GSI is undertaking landslide susceptibility assessments and glaciological studies in the Himalayas, Singh said, adding that these data should be integrated with satellite deformation monitoring, glacial-lake inventories, geophysical studies and flood and debris-flow modelling. GSI studies of nine Himalayan glaciers have recorded overall negative average annual specific mass balance, indicative of substantial glacier mass wastage under changing climatic conditions.

"For India, the appropriate response is not alarm, but science-based preparedness. The objective is not to eliminate the mountains' natural processes, but to understand them better, identify highly vulnerable areas, reduce exposure and improve available response time.

"With sustained scientific monitoring, improved data sharing, appropriate land-use planning, robust infrastructure and community preparedness, risks can be better managed," Singh added.

title: UAE research could provide early warnings to prevent Nepal flooding tragedies - thenationalnews.com
description: UAE research could provide early warnings to prevent Nepal flooding tragedies  thenationalnews.com
publisher.title: thenationalnews.com
full_article:
Abu Dhabi scientists are trying to understand where threats from landslides or glacial collapses may emerge in Nepal as part of research that could save lives.

Their work may offer an early warning to communities at risk from floods prompted by landslides and glacier falls of the kind that last month killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands more missing.

Prof Mohammed Ali and Dr Aisha Al Suwaidi of the department of earth sciences at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi are organising the project, which was set up before the recent tragedy, alongside University of Oxford researcher, Prof Mike Searle.

UAE search and rescue workers find 10 more people missing after Nepal floods Read More Arrow

“If the work helps provide even a few additional minutes of warning, prevents unsafe development in a flood corridor, or improves understanding of where the next hazard may emerge, it will have considerable value,” Dr Al Suwaidi said.

Among the lessons that can be learnt from the recent disaster, the researchers said, is that events in a remote and sparsely populated location “can become a catastrophe much farther downstream”.

“Hazard assessment, therefore, has to follow the entire river system rather than stop at the glacier or national border,” Dr Al Suwaidi added.

The work is part of the Emirates Polar Programme, a research project looking at how the polar regions are being affected by climate change. The Himalayas are part of a region sometimes referred to as the third pole.

There is concern among scientists that the retreat of glaciers and the thawing of permafrost as a result of climate change will make landslides, glacial collapse and floods more likely.

United front

The scientists from Khalifa University are not the only people from the UAE working to help those in Nepal affected by the flooding tragedy.

A UAE Search and Rescue team, working alongside Nepali personnel, have brought the total number of people recovered to 18 since their arrival in the country on September 4.

At least 1,385 have been killed in the floods, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in its latest report. That toll is expected to rise, with 5,130 people still missing, while 13,600 have been rescued so far.

Before the disaster in Nepal, the scientists had started developing their research programme, planning field activities and recruiting researchers, including postgraduate students.

The work, to run over several years, will look at, for example, the region’s climate, changes to the cryosphere (ice, snow and permafrost), outburst floods from glacial lakes and tectonics or movements in the Earth's crust.

The UAE is supporting humanitarian and search-and-rescue operations in Nepal after the horrific natural disaster. Wam Show caption: The UAE is supporting humanitarian and search-and-rescue ope…

Early on, the researchers will analyse historical satellite observations to understand how the landscape has changed.

There will be repeated visits to the area, laboratory analysis and sustained observation of certain glaciers, slopes, lakes and rivers. “The programme brings together modern hazard monitoring and the geological reconstruction of past events,” Prof Ali said.

“This is important because a satellite image or river gauge can tell us what is happening now, whereas sediment and rock can show how frequently comparable events occurred over hundreds, thousands, or millions of years.”

Across the Himalayas in Nepal, glaciers, glacial lakes, snow cover, rivers, unstable slopes and landslide deposits will be mapped repeatedly.

Data from optical and radar satellites will help scientists determine how the area, height and speed of glaciers have changed. It will also help them understand how lakes have appeared and grown, and how landslides or ice dams have formed.

During last month’s disaster, a glacial collapse and a landslide were thought to have blocked a river, with vast quantities of water unleashed when the blockage was breached.

Extreme risk assessment

The devastation, some analysts said, highlighted the need to avoid building in areas at risk of extreme floods.

The importance of early-warning systems was shown by contrasting their absence in Nepal with their sophistication in Switzerland.

In May last year, after scientific analysis indicated that rock falls were putting stress on a glacier above the Swiss village of Blatten, the population was evacuated. Less than two weeks later, a glacial collapse and landslide destroyed the community.

As part of the new UAE research project, the scientists, with partners in Nepal, will select the most at-risk glaciers in need of detailed observations, saying it was not technically nor financially possible to monitor each one closely.

The Seti river at Pokhara, Nepal after it flooded in 2012 because of a landslide made up of rock and ice. Photo: Khalifa University Show caption: The Seti river at Pokhara, Nepal after it flooded in 2012 be…

They will look for accelerated movement of ice, the development of fractures, changes in the levels of lakes, meltwater production and river discharge.

“Continuous monitoring remains sparse across much of Nepal,” Prof Ali said. “No instrument can guarantee that every collapse will be predicted. The purpose is to recognise abnormal changes where possible and to detect events quickly enough to warn downstream communities.”

Analysing, for example, lake sediment and previous deposits from floods and debris flows should provide evidence of former lakes, floods, landslides and earthquakes.

Of particular interest will be the Kathmandu and Pokhara valleys, the latter of which suffered severe flooding in 2012 that killed dozens after an avalanche created a temporary dam in the Seti river that later breached.

Chemical analysis of samples will show how rocks have been uplifted, exposed at the surface and eroded.

“Our goals are both scientific and practical,” Prof Ali said. “Scientifically, we want to understand how climate, glaciers, permafrost, rivers, erosion and tectonics interact across timescales ranging from individual flood events to millions of years.

“Ultimately, success would mean converting scientific observations into usable information: better maps, better monitoring, stronger local expertise, more effective warnings, and safer decisions about where and how infrastructure and communities are developed.”

Perhaps against expectations, the researchers said there was a direct physical connection between the area they were researching and the Arabian Peninsula.

“Dust transported over long distances can settle on Himalayan snow, reduce its reflectivity and increase its absorption of solar energy,” Dr Al Suwaidi said.

“Research has shown that dust can be a major contributor to the darkening and melting of high-altitude snow in high-mountain Asia, particularly above 4,000 metres.

“Some of that dust originates in arid regions of the Middle East, including the Arabian Peninsula. This means the UAE is not simply a distant observer of the third pole: our atmospheric and environmental systems are connected.”

Prof Searle, who is working with the UAE researchers on the project, has four decades of field experience in the Himalayas. He has collected samples while climbing mountains in the region.

He said the ultimate goal was to “understand the whole Himalaya ecosystem in detail” and to reduce the risk of disasters.

“It is very important to understand the whole cryosphere and the processes involved,” he said. “More than one billion people depend on water from the Himalaya. Glaciers are retreating, the permafrost that holds rocks together at altitude is melting. Landslides are becoming increasingly common and glacial lake outburst can be devastating.”
